title: A score board with atomic slots

blocks.text: The page warns that `volatile int[] arr` makes only the **reference** volatile: `arr[0] = 42` is an ordinary write. For element-level guarantees it points to `AtomicIntegerArray`. And a read-modify-write such as `scores[i] += x` is a compound action that `volatile` never makes atomic.
Write `ScoreBoard`, a board of `size` score slots that many threads update:

items: `int update(int slot, IntUnaryOperator change)` applies `change` to the slot's score and returns the new score. Two updates of the **same** slot never lose one another's result. `change` has no side effects, so it may be called again on a fresh value.
An update of one slot never waits for an update of a **different** slot.
`int get(int slot)` reads one score; `int[] snapshot()` copies all of them.

rows: slot 1 is 0; one thread adds 10 while another adds 1

cases.says: Each update applies its change to one slot and returns that slot's new score.
Two updates of the same slot at the same time are both kept; neither overwrites the other.
An update of one slot does not wait for an update of another slot that is still running.

concepts: A volatile array reference does not make its elements volatile; AtomicIntegerArray gives element-level guarantees.
An update of one element that reads and writes it must be atomic, or a concurrent update is lost.
